cards.confidenceNote: Moscow arrival from Al Jazeera (AP, Reuters); three-leader meeting status from China's 4 November foreign-ministry remarks; no White House confirmation found.
cards.title: US envoys meet Putin as APEC three-way meeting stays unconfirmed
cards.summary: Witkoff and Kushner reached Moscow on 12 November after the Abu Dhabi talks ended. Trump expects to meet Putin and Xi at APEC in Shenzhen on 18-19 November, but neither Washington nor Beijing has confirmed it. China's two-month truce extension runs to 10 January.
cards.body:
The diplomacy between Washington, Moscow and Beijing now runs on three clocks. The first is Moscow: Witkoff and Kushner flew there on 12 November, straight from Abu Dhabi, and were met at the plane by Kirill Dmitriev, Putin's investment envoy and the Kremlin's preferred channel to Trump's team. Al Jazeera's Moscow correspondent says they carry an updated peace proposal and want Putin to accept a European role, which he has refused.

The second clock is APEC in Shenzhen on 18-19 November. Trump has said he expects to meet both Xi and Putin there. Beijing's line has not moved since 4 November, when its foreign ministry said it was maintaining communication about a three-leader meeting, and the White House has confirmed nothing. A three-way meeting would be the first of its kind and would put the Ukraine settlement and the US-China trade truce on the same table, which is what Moscow wants and what European governments fear.

The third clock is the trade truce. China's commerce ministry extended its suspension of the expanded export controls to 10 January, which Reuters described as a pause on rare-earth curbs. That removes the 10 November cliff but sets a new one in the middle of winter.

Outside the summitry, the record shows strain rather than alignment. The Russia-led CSTO stripped Armenia of its voting rights over unpaid dues, a sign that Moscow's own bloc is fraying at its edge. Two Chinese-built heavy-lift ships used for the sanctioned Arctic LNG 2 project now sit under Russian ownership and flag, gCaptain reported from vessel records. And the Nvidia spy affair, in which an alleged Chinese agent is accused of targeting Jensen Huang, remains a press story rather than an official action, apart from Trump saying the FBI is investigating.

Assessment (inference): a confirmed Shenzhen meeting would raise great-power stakes in both directions, because it could bring a Ukraine framework or expose how far apart the three still are. Until one capital confirms it, the board treats it as Trump's expectation, not a scheduled event. Watch for a White House schedule, a Chinese foreign-ministry announcement, and whether Putin's answer to the envoys includes any opening for Europe.

cards.confidenceNote: Arrest from UK police statements via Military Times and DW, unit detail via AP; Fairford charges from the US Justice Department via BBC and France 24; summons via DW and The New Arab.
cards.title: US soldier held in Britain on suspicion of spying for Russia
cards.summary: British police arrested a 41-year-old US Army member near Gloucester on suspicion of spying for Russia; AP reports he served in NATO's Allied Rapid Reaction Corps. The US charged three Iran-backed operatives over a plot at RAF Fairford, and France summoned Iran's ambassador over cyberattacks.
cards.body:
Three espionage and sabotage cases moved into the courts or the diplomatic record in two days, and all of them touch Britain or a NATO ally.

The first is an arrest inside NATO. On 10 November counter-terrorism police arrested a 41-year-old US Army member near Gloucester under the National Security Act, on suspicion of assisting a foreign intelligence service; police said the country concerned is Russia. US, NATO and British officials told the AP he served in NATO's Allied Rapid Reaction Corps at Imjin Barracks, a UK-led headquarters with personnel from about 20 nations. FBI Director Kash Patel and Army counter-intelligence commented on the record. No charge has been announced, and police say the case is unrelated to the Fairford plot.

The second is a US indictment. The Justice Department charged three Iran-backed operatives in an eight-count indictment that includes conspiracy to provide material support to Kataib Hezbollah and the Revolutionary Guard, and alleges one of them orchestrated a plot at RAF Fairford, the British base from which US bombers flew before leaving in September. It is the first US charging step tied to Iranian activity against a base on allied soil during this war, and it follows the US move of tankers out of RAF Mildenhall on 9 November.

The third is diplomatic. France summoned Iran's ambassador on 10 November over the October cyberattacks on supermarket refrigeration that Paris blames on the Guard's Shahid Kaveh unit; Iran denies involvement. France says it will seek EU sanctions, which would be the first EU listing over Iranian cyber sabotage in Europe.

Russia answered in kind on 11 November: the FSB said it had arrested two alleged Polish agents in Kaliningrad, a claim Warsaw called disinformation. And Britain put money behind its undersea defences, launching the £90m Atlantic Net to track Russian submarines and protect cables from 2027.

Assessment (inference): the pattern is a hardening counter-intelligence front in Europe, with Iran now treated alongside Russia as a source of physical and cyber sabotage. Watch for a charge in the Gloucester case, any EU listing over the French attacks, and further arrests linked to bases used in the Iran war.

cards.confidenceNote: Strike pause rests on no reports of a US strike since 6-7 November in wire and directory coverage; Fairford charges via BBC and France 24; Bessent via anonymous sources only.
cards.title: No US strike on Iran since 7 November as blockade stays
cards.summary: No US strike on Iranian territory has been reported since the Qeshm strikes of 6-7 November, and Trump calls more strikes unlikely. The blockade remains in force. Iran showed an underground missile site, and Saudi Arabia raised output to 10.56 million barrels a day in October.
cards.body:
The kinetic war with Iran is in a pause, not an end. The last reported US strikes on Iranian territory were the air-defence targets on Qeshm on 2 November and again on 6-7 November, which Trump called minor. Since then the record shows no strike day, and on 9 November Trump said further strikes are 'quite unlikely' and the war is 'militarily effectively over'. The blockade is the instrument that remains: US aircraft disabled the blockade runner Huda on 7 November and CENTCOM's Task Force Iron Gate now targets land and Caspian routes.

Iran's side of the ledger is defiance. Iranian media on 10 November showed the armed forces chief of staff and the Guard's aerospace commander touring a new underground 'missile city' at an undisclosed location, days after a lawmaker called for longer-range missiles able to reach European bases. The Guard's claims that tankers hit mines on an 'unauthorised' route remain unconfirmed by any maritime authority or owner.

The more active front is now abroad. The US charged three Iran-backed operatives over a plot at RAF Fairford, Treasury Secretary Bessent reportedly moved to a military base over Iranian threats, and the US had already moved tankers out of RAF Mildenhall. France has summoned Iran's ambassador over cyber sabotage.

On energy, OPEC's November report shows how much the market has adjusted: Saudi Arabia pumped 10.56 million barrels a day in October, its highest since the war began, and OPEC+ output rose about 2 million barrels a day to 41.23 million. More supply from outside the Strait reduces the price leverage Iran gains from keeping Hormuz contested.

Assessment (inference): the absence of strikes lowers the near-term chance of a direct exchange. The kinetic axis sits at 75, inside the band for a formal blockade and multiple disrupted chokepoints, because the blockade is enforced by fire and Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia continue; nothing in the record is a direct clash between major powers. Watch for any US strike or interception, a maritime authority confirming a mine hit, and new threats against US officials or bases.

cards.confidenceNote: Qatar meeting and Rubio's account from AFP/AP via Arab News and Euronews (9 November); no talks scheduled in any read source; Syria and GCC items from the New York Times and The New Arab.
cards.title: No US delegation has joined Iran talks since Qatar visit
cards.summary: No US delegation has joined talks with Iran since Qatar's prime minister met Trump on 9 November; Rubio reported no progress and Iran repeats its seven conditions. Gulf states approved a joint command headquarters in Kuwait, and Syria is weighing troops to help Saudi Arabia against the Houthis.
cards.body:
The diplomatic track with Iran has gone quiet since Qatar's prime minister met Trump and Vance at the White House on 9 November. Trump came out of that meeting saying the war is effectively over; Rubio said there was no progress, and Iran's Rezaei told Washington to accept Iran's seven conditions. In the three days since, no read source reports a US delegation joining talks, in Doha or elsewhere, and no new Qatari proposal has been published.

The gap is the sequence. Reporting before the Washington meeting described a Qatari plan that pairs blockade relief and IAEA access with a reopening of Hormuz under an Iran-Oman arrangement; who moves first has not been settled in public. While that holds, the Strait stays contested and the blockade stays on.

Meanwhile, the Gulf is building its own security architecture. GCC defence ministers approved an advanced headquarters in Kuwait for their unified military command and a force deployment to it, without giving a size. Syria is weighing sending thousands of troops to Saudi Arabia and Yemen against the Houthis, possibly under the Mecca defence pact with Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan, Syrian and Yemeni officials told the New York Times; no decision has been made. Turkey and Iraq agreed that Turkish forces will hand over the Bashiqa base in northern Iraq.

Europe has entered the Iran file on its own terms. France summoned Iran's ambassador over cyber sabotage and wants EU sanctions; the US indictment over the Fairford plot puts Britain in the same frame. Those moves narrow the space for a quick deal that rewards Tehran with relief.

Assessment (inference): mediation is waiting on a sequencing concession neither side has made, and regional states are hedging by building collective defence that relies less on US bases. Watch for a US delegation in Doha, any Iranian reply to Qatar, an EU decision on listings, and whether Syria commits troops.

cards.confidenceNote: Mandate from The Guardian and the NYT (7 Nov); recommendation count and unity-government exchange from Ynet via research return (not a directory outlet), stated as reported.
cards.title: Herzog asks Eisenkot to form Israel's next government
cards.summary: President Herzog gave opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot the mandate to form a government on 7 November after more lawmakers recommended him than Netanyahu. Netanyahu remains caretaker prime minister and has called for a unity government; Eisenkot's camp rejects it in its current form.
cards.body:
Israel's post-election deadlock has its first formal step. President Isaac Herzog gave Gadi Eisenkot, a former military chief of staff who leads the opposition camp, the mandate to form a government on 7 November, after more Knesset members recommended him than Netanyahu (The Guardian; New York Times). Eisenkot has 28 days, extendable by 14, to assemble a majority. The election on 27 October gave Netanyahu's bloc 53 of 120 seats, Eisenkot's camp 48 and Arab-majority parties a record 19, so no bloc holds 61 without crossing lines its members have drawn.

Netanyahu remains caretaker prime minister with full authority over military operations, including decisions on Iran. He has called for a national unity government; Eisenkot's side says it will not join one in its current form and wants Likud to drop its far-right partners, according to Israeli reporting. Herzog said the next government must advance the US 20-point Gaza plan through the Board of Peace, and Trump publicly told Netanyahu to stop obstructing it. Israel's Shin Bet reportedly found no evidence of foreign interference in the election, after Netanyahu's camp had alleged fraud.

For the Iran war, the change matters through command authority. Israeli reporting last week said Netanyahu and the Mossad chief had planned an operation against Iran on the eve of the election that was halted after the US was told; that report is disputed. A caretaker government can still act, but a transition to an Eisenkot-led coalition would put a former chief of staff who has been critical of open-ended operations in charge of the Iran and Lebanon files.

In Lebanon, Israeli drone strikes continue in the south; Lebanon's health ministry reported one person killed on 4 November in Qabrikha, and Prime Minister Nawaf Salam warned against Lebanon being drawn into a renewed US-Iran war.

What to watch: whether Eisenkot can win over ultra-Orthodox or Arab-backed support; any unity-government talks; caretaker decisions on Iran or Lebanon during the mandate; and the Gaza plan's progress.

cards.confidenceNote: Talks outcome from The Guardian, France 24 and Al Jazeera; Moscow visit from Al Jazeera; Iran charges and summons from BBC, France 24, DW and The New Arab.
cards.title: US envoys take Ukraine plan to Putin as Iran plot charges filed
cards.summary: The Abu Dhabi talks ended with a prisoner deal and the US envoys flew to Moscow to meet Putin. On Iran, strikes have paused while the US charged Iran-backed plotters over a British base and France summoned Iran's ambassador. The headline risk score holds at 65.
cards.body:
Both of the board's war arcs are now run through envoys rather than strikes, and both are producing friction with Europe.

On Ukraine, two days of talks in Abu Dhabi produced a prisoner exchange of more than 1,000 per side and what Ukraine called progress on security guarantees, but nothing on territory. The envoys went straight to Moscow to put an updated proposal to Putin, and only afterwards to Dublin to brief Zelensky and European leaders. European governments are outside the core format, and Estonia's prime minister says Putin does not get to choose Europe's negotiators. Russia kept striking Ukraine before and after the talks, and Ukraine hit Omsk and Ust-Luga.

On Iran, the US has not struck Iranian territory since 6-7 November and Trump calls more strikes unlikely, while the blockade stays. The pressure has moved to courts and capitals: a US indictment over a plot at RAF Fairford, France's summons of Iran's ambassador over cyber sabotage, and reported threats that moved the Treasury Secretary to a military base.

The shared thread is NATO's European flank. A US soldier was arrested in Britain on suspicion of spying for Russia; Ukrainian drones strayed over Lithuania and Estonia; Russia's FSB claims to have caught Polish agents; Britain is funding new submarine and cable surveillance. None of these breaks an alliance commitment, but they keep Europe's security agenda separate from Washington's deal-making.

The score: the board has applied its November methodology audits to the live axes. Kinetic is 75, the band for a formal blockade and multiple disrupted chokepoints, short of direct major-power fighting; great-power is 70, reflecting Russia's attacks on shipping in NATO members' Black Sea waters; nuclear posture is 60; alliance is 60, because the US cut joint drills with South Korea in August and has not restored them. The mean is 66. The change from 65 is a correction of method, not a new escalation.

Assessment (inference): the next seven days turn on Putin's answer to the envoys and on APEC. A confirmed three-leader meeting or a ceasefire framework would move great-power risk; a new US strike on Iran or a mass Russian missile day would move kinetic risk up. A second week without US strikes on Iran would not move the axis while the blockade holds.

cards.confidenceNote: Talks outcome from The Guardian, France 24, Al Jazeera and NPR; Kyiv strike counts from the Ukrainian Air Force via Kyiv Independent; Moldova from Moldovan authorities via Kyiv Independent.
cards.title: Abu Dhabi talks end with prisoner deal, no territorial breakthrough
cards.summary: Russia and Ukraine agreed in Abu Dhabi on the war's largest prisoner exchange, over 1,000 per side, but not on territory. US envoys took an updated proposal to Putin on 12 November. Russia struck Kyiv with a ballistic missile and 123 drones; Ukraine hit Omsk and Ust-Luga.
cards.body:
The first US-mediated talks in nine months ended on 11 November with one deliverable and one unresolved core. The deliverable is a prisoner exchange that Kushner said would involve more than 1,000 people from each side, the largest of the war. Ukraine's David Arakhamia reported 'really big progress' on post-war security guarantees and spoke of momentum toward a solution before the new year. The core is territory: Russia's team came with what Arakhamia called very strict directives, Moscow still demands the rest of Donetsk and all of Donbas, and Zelensky rules out concessions.

The format remains a US shuttle. Witkoff and Kushner flew to Moscow on 12 November and were met by Kirill Dmitriev; they then go to Dublin, where more than 40 European leaders met at the European Political Community, to brief Zelensky. Europe is not at the table. Estonia's prime minister says Putin does not get to choose Europe's negotiators, as some capitals debate whether Kallas should represent the EU.

The fighting did not pause. On 11 November Russia launched a Kh-59/69 missile, 163 drones and Banderol cruise missiles; two Banderols crossed Moldova's airspace for several minutes, and strikes killed nine people across Ukraine that day. Hours after the talks closed, Russia struck Kyiv with an Iskander-M and 123 drones, killing one person. Ukraine attacked Omsk, home to Russia's largest refinery, for more than eight hours, and hit Ust-Luga, where Estonia's defence minister said a Baltic Fleet vessel was damaged. Drones on the Ust-Luga route strayed over Lithuania and Estonia, and NATO jets failed to bring one down. Rosneft has capped fuel sales in at least four Russian regions.

Assessment (inference): the prisoner deal builds trust but does not close the territorial gap that has blocked every round. The next markers are Putin's reply to the envoys, the timing of the exchange, and whether either side offers a limited energy or maritime ceasefire. Neither side has announced one. A failure in Moscow would likely bring a heavier Russian strike; Ukraine's long-range campaign on refineries looks set to continue regardless.

iran_lead.title: US charges Iran-backed plotters over British base as strikes pause
iran_lead.summary: The US Justice Department charged three Iran-backed operatives, alleging one orchestrated a plot at RAF Fairford, a British base used by US bombers. France summoned Iran's ambassador over cyberattacks on supermarkets, and Treasury Secretary Bessent reportedly moved to a military base over Iranian threats. No US strike on Iran has been reported since 7 November.
facts: 10 November: an eight-count US indictment charged three Iran-backed operatives, one accused of orchestrating a plot at RAF Fairford (BBC; France 24).
10 November: France summoned Iran's ambassador over the supermarket cyberattacks; Iran denies a role (DW; The New Arab).
11 November: Bessent moved to a military base over Iranian threats, people familiar said; Treasury did not confirm the move (Times of Israel; Al Jazeera).
10 November: Iranian media showed commanders touring an underground 'missile city' at an undisclosed site (Iran International).
October: Saudi Arabia pumped 10.56 million barrels a day, its most since the war began, OPEC said (Al Jazeera).
No US strike on Iranian territory has been reported since the Qeshm strikes of 6-7 November; the blockade remains in force.
iran_lead.changed: The confrontation has moved away from the Gulf battlefield: no new US strike has been reported since 6-7 November and Trump calls more strikes unlikely, while the blockade stays in force. The new activity is in the West: US charges over a plot at a British base, France's summons of Iran's ambassador, and reported threats that moved Bessent to a base. Iran showed off an underground missile site, and Saudi output rose to its highest since the war began.
iran_lead.watch: Whether a US delegation joins talks through Qatar; any US strike or new blockade interception; further charges or arrests tied to Iran in Europe; EU action after France's summons; confirmation of the Guard's tanker-mine claims; Houthi fire on Saudi Arabia.

brics_lead.title: US envoys meet Putin as APEC three-leader meeting stays unconfirmed
brics_lead.summary: Witkoff and Kushner arrived in Moscow on 12 November after the Abu Dhabi talks. Neither the White House nor Beijing has confirmed the Trump-Putin-Xi meeting Trump expects at APEC in Shenzhen on 18-19 November. In Britain, police arrested a US Army member on suspicion of spying for Russia, and the Russia-led CSTO stripped Armenia of its vote.
brics_lead.changed: The US channel to Moscow moved from the negotiating table to the Kremlin, a week before APEC, while China still says only that it is in communication about a three-leader meeting. Counter-intelligence cases landed on both sides of NATO's eastern edge: a US soldier held in Britain over Russia, and an FSB claim of Polish agents in Kaliningrad that Warsaw calls disinformation. Britain launched a programme to track Russian submarines.
brics_lead.watch: Whether the White House or Beijing confirms a Shenzhen meeting; APEC on 18-19 November; the Quad summit date in Manila; charges in the British spy case; China's response to the Nvidia spy affair; North Korean launches.

facts: 12 November: Witkoff and Kushner arrived in Moscow to meet Putin (Al Jazeera).
4 November: China's foreign ministry said it is maintaining communication on a three-leader meeting; no confirmation since.
10 November: a 41-year-old US Army member was arrested near Gloucester on suspicion of spying for Russia (Military Times; DW).
11 November: the FSB said it arrested two alleged Polish agents in Kaliningrad; Poland called it disinformation (The Moscow Times).
11 November: Britain launched the £90m Atlantic Net to track Russian submarines and protect cables (gCaptain).
11 November: the CSTO stripped Armenia of its voting rights over unpaid dues (The Moscow Times).

ukraine_lead.title: Abu Dhabi talks end with prisoner swap as US envoys meet Putin
ukraine_lead.summary: Two days of US-mediated talks in Abu Dhabi ended on 11 November with agreement on the war's largest prisoner exchange, more than 1,000 from each side, but no breakthrough on territory. Witkoff and Kushner flew to Moscow on 12 November to meet Putin, hours after Russia struck Kyiv with a ballistic missile and 123 drones.
facts: 11 November: the talks ended with a prisoner exchange of more than 1,000 per side, Kushner said; Ukraine's Arakhamia reported progress on security guarantees (The Guardian; France 24).
Arakhamia said Russia's team arrived with 'very, very strict directives'; Kyiv rejects Moscow's demand for all of Donbas (The Guardian; Al Jazeera).
12 November: Dmitriev met Witkoff and Kushner at their plane in Moscow; they go on to Dublin to brief Zelensky and European leaders (Al Jazeera).
12 November: one Iskander-M and 123 drones at Ukraine; one killed and seven injured in Kyiv (Kyiv Independent).
11 November: two Russian cruise missiles crossed Moldovan airspace for four to five minutes (Kyiv Independent).
11 November: Ukrainian drones attacked Omsk, home to Russia's largest refinery, and Ust-Luga, where a Baltic Fleet vessel was hit (Kyiv Independent; ERR News).
ukraine_lead.changed: The talks produced their first concrete result, a prisoner exchange, and Ukraine reported progress on post-war security guarantees, but the territorial gap is unchanged: Russia still demands all of Donbas and Zelensky refuses. Europe stays outside the room; the envoys will brief European leaders in Dublin after Moscow. Strikes continued on both sides, and two Russian cruise missiles crossed Moldova's airspace.
ukraine_lead.watch: What Putin tells the envoys, including on any European role; when the prisoner exchange begins; EU ministers' expected adoption of new sanctions on 16 November; another mass missile strike; more Ukrainian drones straying over the Baltic states.
